extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students / contest-oriented readers learning basic group theory and metric topology
extracted.subtask_short: learning basic group and metric theory
extracted.subtask_description: Study and apply foundational definitions, propositions, and examples about groups (isomorphisms, orders, subgroups, small-group classification) and metric spaces (metrics, convergence, continuity, open/closed sets, product metric, homeomorphisms). Includes exercises and illustrative examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness of identity and inverses; inverse of inverse
rubrics_metrics.description: Fact 1.2.3. (a) The identity of a group is unique. (b) The inverse of any element is unique. (c) For any g ∈ G, (g^{-1})^{-1} = g.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short formal manipulations show these properties; proofs given/sketched: if 1 and 1' are identities then 1 = 1 ⋆ 1' = 1'; if h and h' are inverses to g then h' = (h' ⋆ g) ⋆ h = 1_G ⋆ h = h. Item (c) is trivial/omitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inverse of a product
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposition 1.2.4 (Inverse of products): For a group G and a,b ∈ G, (ab)^{-1} = b^{-1} a^{-1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct computation: show (ab)(b^{-1} a^{-1}) = 1_G and (b^{-1} a^{-1})(ab) = 1_G, hence equality of inverses. This demonstrates standard manipulation rules useful in proofs involving inverses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Left multiplication is a bijection (cancellation law)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lemma 1.2.5: For a group G and fixed g ∈ G, the map x ↦ g x from G to G is a bijection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check injectivity and surjectivity directly (Exercise 1.2.6). The injectivity aspect is often called the cancellation law; examples (e.g., multiplication by 3 on (Z/7Z)^×) illustrate bijectivity explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isomorphism of groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition 1.3.1: A bijection φ : G → H is an isomorphism if φ(g1 ⋆ g2) = φ(g1) * φ(g2) for all g1, g2 ∈ G. If such φ exists write G ≅ H.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Isomorphisms reassign 'names' of elements while preserving structure. Examples: Z ≅ 10Z via x ↦ 10x; G×H ≅ H×G via (g,h) ↦ (h,g); identity map id: G→G is an isomorphism; negation on Z is an automorphism. Nontrivial example: mapping Z/6Z to (Z/7Z)^× via a mod 6 ↦ 3^a mod 7 when 3 is a primitive root.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of a group and order of an element
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition 1.4.1: The order |G| of a group G is its number of elements (may be infinite). Definition 1.4.3: The order of an element g is the smallest positive n with g^n = 1_G, or ∞ if none.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: |(Z/pZ)^×| = p-1; order of -1 in Q^× is 2; order of 1 in Z is infinite. Exercises ask for orders in small cyclic groups and connect to number-theoretic notions (primitive roots).

rubrics_metrics.name: If g^n = 1 then ord(g) divides n / finiteness of element order
rubrics_metrics.description: Fact 1.4.7: If g^n = 1_G then ord g divides n. Fact 1.4.8: In a finite group G every element has finite order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard divisibility property (use smallest exponent). For finite groups, use pigeonhole/sequence 1_G, g, g^2, ... to find repetition, hence finite order. These are foundational facts used repeatedly (e.g., Fermat's little theorem as special case).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lagrange-type exponent theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 1.4.9 (Lagrange’s theorem for orders): For any finite group G and any x ∈ G, x^{|G|} = 1_G.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Important result; proof later in generality of Theorem 3.4.1. Keep this result in mind for element orders and applications in number theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of subgroup and subgroup remarks
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition 1.5.1: A subgroup of G = (G, ⋆) is a group H = (H, ⋆) where H ⊆ G (operation inherited). Proper subgroup means H ≠ G. Remark 1.5.2: To specify a subgroup it suffices to specify its elements; the operation is inherited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 2Z ⊆ Z; stabilizer-like subsets in S_n; {(g,1_H) | g ∈ G} in G×H. Trivial subgroup {1_G} and G itself always subgroups. Non-examples illustrate failure modes (missing inverses, not closed under operation, empty set lacks identity). Exercises check subgroup generated by an element ⟨x⟩ and its relation with ord x.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subgroup generated by a set / element
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition/Example 3.1.1 / 1.5.5: For S ⊆ G, ⟨S⟩ is the set of finite products of elements of S and their inverses. For a single x, ⟨x⟩ = {..., x^{-2}, x^{-1}, 1, x, x^2, ...}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If ⟨S⟩ = G then S generates G. Exercises: determine ⟨x⟩ when ord x = 2015 or infinite. Pedagogical metaphor: put generators in a box and produce all finite words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification list of groups of small orders (≤10) up to isomorphism
rubrics_metrics.description: List: order 1 trivial; order 2 Z/2Z; order 3 Z/3Z; order 4 Z/4Z and Z/2Z×Z/2Z (Klein four); order 5 Z/5Z; order 6 Z/6Z and S_3 (≅ D_6); order 7 Z/7Z; order 8 many: Z/8Z, Z/4Z×Z/2Z, Z/2Z×Z/2Z×Z/2Z, D_8, Q_8; order 9 Z/9Z and Z/3Z×Z/3Z; order 10 Z/10Z (≅ Z/5Z×Z/2Z) and D_{10}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are all groups up to isomorphism for those orders; comments show where certain familiar groups appear (Chinese remainder theorem, dihedral vs symmetric groups). Useful as quick reference and for examples/non-examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metric space definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition 2.1.1: A metric space is (M,d) with d: M×M → R_{≥0} satisfying: symmetry d(x,y)=d(y,x); positive definiteness d(x,y)≥0 with equality iff x=y; triangle inequality d(x,z)+d(z,y) ≥ d(x,y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abuse-of-notation: often write M for (M,d). Many examples follow: R with |x-y|, R^2 with Euclidean metric, taxicab metric, discrete metric, graphs as metric spaces, function spaces with integral norm. Visualization encouraged; draw pictures for new objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convergence in metric spaces (epsilon definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition 2.2.1: A sequence (x_n) in metric space M converges to x if ∀ε>0 ∃N such that for all n≥N, d(x_n,x) < ε. Denote x_n → x or lim_{n→∞} x_n = x.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convergence is relative to the parent space M (limits must lie in M). Example: sequence of decimal approximations converges to √2 in R but does not converge in Q. Exercise about convergent sequences in discrete metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity for metric spaces (epsilon-delta) and equivalence with sequential continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition 2.3.2: f: M→N is continuous at p if ∀ε>0 ∃δ>0 s.t. d_M(x,p)<δ ⇒ d_N(f(x),f(p))<ε. Theorem 2.3.3: f is continuous at p iff it preserves limits of sequences converging to p (sequential continuity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof sketch: ε-δ ⇒ sequential continuity (exercise). Conversely, failure of ε-δ gives a 'bad' ε and a sequence showing sequential discontinuity. Use sequential continuity for simpler proofs (e.g., composition of continuous maps).

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of continuous functions is continuous
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposition 2.3.5: If f: M→N and g: N→L are continuous, then g∘f is continuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via sequences: if x_n → p then f(x_n)→f(p) then g(f(x_n))→g(f(p)). Simple application of sequential characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homeomorphism / topological equivalence for metric spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition 2.4.1: A bijection f: M→N is a homeomorphism if both f and f^{-1} are continuous. M and N are homeomorphic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require continuity of inverse because a continuous bijection need not have continuous inverse (examples: continuous bijection [0,1)→circle without continuous inverse; discrete space of size |R| maps continuously into R without continuous inverse). Examples: S^1 ≅ boundary of unit square; (−1,1) ≅ R via tan map. Homeomorphisms capture 'continuous deformations'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product metric and equivalence of common metrics on product spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition 2.5.2 and preceding: On M×N one can use d_max, d_Euclid (sqrt sum squares), or d_taxicab (sum). Exercise/inequality: d_max ≤ d_Euclid ≤ d_taxicab ≤ 2 d_max; any of these give homeomorphic metrics; refer to 'product metric'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposition 2.5.4: Convergence in product metric is componentwise: (x_n,y_n)→(x,y) iff x_n→x and y_n→y. Use product metric to show continuity of addition and multiplication R×R→R via componentwise arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open sets (neighborhood definition) and open-set characterization of continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition 2.6.1/2.6.3: Mr(p) = {x: d(x,p)<r} is an r-neighborhood. U⊆M is open if for each p∈U some r-neighborhood Mr(p) ⊆ U. Theorem 2.6.11: f: M→N is continuous iff preimage of every open set in N is open in M.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: open intervals and open balls; empty set and whole space are open. Non-examples: closed interval [0,1] not open in R. Propositions: finite intersections and arbitrary unions of open sets are open. Exercises: infinite intersection example producing {0}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed sets, limit points, and complements of open sets
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition 2.7.1: S⊆M is closed if whenever a sequence (x_n) in S converges to x in M, then x∈S. Define lim S = {limits of sequences from S} (closure S = lim S). Theorem 2.7.7: S closed iff M\S is open.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: closed interval [0,1] closed in R; empty and whole space are closed. Non-examples: (0,1) not closed in R. Exercises to show closure properties and to visualize complements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abuse of notation and conventional shorthand
rubrics_metrics.description: Several 'abuse of notation' notes: identity sometimes denoted 0 instead of 1 in additive groups; (M,d) often abbreviated to M; 'converges in M' abbreviated to 'converges' when parent space is understood; metric on subset inherited and notation shortened accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These notational conventions are cautioned about early: be aware convergence/ openness/closedness are relative to parent space; notation choices (additive vs multiplicative identity) depend on context and intended intuition.
